paragraphs.heading: A partnership at the root
paragraphs.text: A mycorrhiza is a partnership between a fungus and a plant in which the fungus's hyphae and the plant's roots grow together and meet at the level of cells. The name comes from Greek words for fungus and root. The fungus settles into the root tissue, either inside the cells, as arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi do, or outside them, as ectomycorrhizal fungi do. The relationship is normally good for both sides.

paragraphs.heading: Food for minerals
paragraphs.text: The plant makes organic molecules by photosynthesis and passes some to the fungus as sugars or lipids. In return, the fungus brings the plant water and minerals from the soil, such as phosphorus, nitrogen or zinc. Mycorrhizae have important roles in feeding plants and in the biology and chemistry of soil. In some species or situations, though, the fungus can act as a parasite on its host.

paragraphs.heading: Common across plants
paragraphs.text: Most plant species form mycorrhizae, although some families, such as Brassicaceae and Chenopodiaceae, cannot. The arbuscular type is the most common, found in 70% of plant species, including many crops such as cereals and legumes. Mycorrhizae sit in the roots of vascular plants, but similar partnerships also occur in bryophytes.

paragraphs.heading: How it was found
paragraphs.text: The German botanist Frank first formally described and named these fungi in 1885, and he coined the word mycorrhiza. Others had already noticed the link. In 1881 Franciszek Kamieński showed that the plant Monotropa hypopitys fed through fungi from neighboring trees. In 1899 Noël Bernard found that orchids such as Neottia nidus-avis need a particular fungus for their seeds to sprout.

paragraphs.heading: Helping plants onto land
paragraphs.text: Fossil and genetic evidence suggest mycorrhizae arose as early as 450-500 million years ago. Before plants reached land, soils held few nutrients and plants had not yet evolved roots. Without roots, early land plants could not pull stubborn nutrients such as phosphate out of minerals. Researchers who study ancient fungi broadly agree that these fungi acted as a simple root system for the first land plants. Research suggests they were a key factor in letting plants settle on land at all.

paragraphs.heading: Clues in ancient stone
paragraphs.text: The oldest direct fossil evidence comes from the Rhynie chert, rock 407 million years old that holds very well preserved plants colonized by fungi. In it, fungi sit inside the cells of the plants Aglaophyton major and Horneophyton lignieri. Structures for swapping nutrients, called arbuscules and hyphal coils, survive in the fossils, and the colonized cells seem to have been alive, which points to a partnership that helped both sides. Scientists call these links mycorrhiza-like, since true mycorrhizae are defined by fungi in roots and these early plants had none.

paragraphs.heading: Newer kinds of partnership
paragraphs.text: Arbuscular mycorrhizae came first, and other types, such as ectomycorrhizae, appeared when plants switched to partnering with different groups of fungi. Ectomycorrhizae are thought to have begun among early relatives of the Pinaceae about 175 million years ago, though the oldest fossil of them, on Pinus roots, is 48.7 million years old. Ericoid mycorrhizae are the youngest type, dating to around 118 million years ago. The ability to form mycorrhizae goes back to the ancestor of all land plants, and lineages without it, such as Brassicaceae, lost it along the way.
